title: Human Heart Mini Unit Study (Stephanie Hathaway Designs)
dropperComment: Mini Study for pre-k to young elementary. love the art styles and array of activities

unmappedSkills.description: Identify and name the main parts of the human heart (aorta, ventricles, atria, valves, veins, arteries, vena cava)
Understand that the heart pumps blood through the body via the circulatory system (heart, veins, arteries, capillaries)
Know basic components of blood (red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, plasma) and their functions

difficulty.multiAgeNotes: Designed to span Pre-K through elementary. Younger kids: coloring pages, letter pages, read-aloud info card. Older kids: labeling diagrams, vocabulary, word search, copy work, independent reading.

appealDrivers: dual art styles (realistic watercolor + simplified cross-section)

printFormat.colorRequirement: color optional — many pages work in B&W
printFormat.mixedOrientationNotes: Most pages portrait, info card is landscape (5x7 printable)

gaps: unit-study-packet: multi-page themed study bundle containing 8-12 different activity types all centered on one topic. Template structure: cover → teacher guide → reference posters (labeled/unlabeled/B&W) → info card → vocabulary list → letter tracing → labeled diagram → blank labeling activity → cross-section diagram (labeled/unlabeled) → flow diagram with arrows → coloring page → cut-and-assemble craft → word search.

labeled-anatomy-diagram: scientific illustration with numbered leader lines pointing to parts, word bank at bottom. Scaffolded versions: fully labeled → numbered with word bank → completely blank for testing.
cut-and-assemble-craft: page of labeled cutout pieces that student colors, cuts, and assembles into a 3D model or layered diagram. Combines art + motor skills + spatial reasoning + content knowledge.

components.name: Cover Page
components.description: Title page with beautiful watercolor anatomical heart illustration. 'Human Heart Mini Unit Study' title in script font.
designPatterns: Gallery-quality cover sets tone: this is beautiful, not clinical

components.name: Teacher/Parent Guide (p2-3)
components.description: Two-page written guide explaining all included materials and how to use them across age ranges. Suggests adaptations: read-aloud for younger, copy work for older, artwork inspiration for all.

components.name: Anatomical Posters — Watercolor Style (p4-8)
components.description: 5 versions of the same watercolor heart illustration: (1) numbered with word bank, (2) fully labeled inline, (3) unlabeled color poster, (4) numbered B&W with word bank, (5) unlabeled B&W (coloring page). Frameable quality.
designPatterns: Scaffolded versions: labeled → numbered → blank = teach → practice → test
Watercolor art style: pen-and-ink linework with watercolor washes in anatomical reds/blues/purples
Poster-quality: 'pretty enough to frame' — designed to hang on wall as reference

components.name: 5x7 Info Card (p11)
components.description: Landscape info card with heart illustration on left, key facts on right. Simple language for read-aloud. Covers: heart as muscle, circulatory system, heartbeats per day, blood composition, blood functions.
designPatterns: Dual-purpose: reference + copy work for older students

components.name: Vocabulary Page (p12)
components.description: Glossary of heart-related terms: aorta, artery, blood pressure, capillaries, cardiologist, cardiology, circulatory system, etc. Simple definitions.
designPatterns: Copy work source for older students

components.name: Letter Pages — H for Heart (p13-14)
components.description: Full-page uppercase H and lowercase h outlines with small heart illustration. For letter recognition, tracing, or coloring.

components.name: Vocabulary Tracing (p15)
components.description: Dotted-line tracing words: heart, artery, vein, blood, heartbeat, pump, cells. Three-line handwriting guide (top, middle, baseline).
designPatterns: Dotted letter tracing on three-line guide

components.name: Cross-Section Diagrams — Simplified Style (p16-19)
components.description: Simplified, color-coded cross-section of heart (different art style from watercolor posters). 4 versions: (1) labeled, (2) labeled with blood flow arrows, (3) blank B&W coloring page, (4) unlabeled with blank lines for labeling. Color-coded: reds/pinks for oxygenated, blues for deoxygenated, oranges for veins.
designPatterns: Second art style: simplified/graphic vs. realistic watercolor
Blood flow arrows show function, not just structure

components.name: Cut-and-Assemble Heart Craft (p20-21)
components.description: Two pages: (1) labeled cutout pieces for each heart part (left ventricle, right ventricle, left atrium, right atrium, aorta, valves, pulmonary artery/vein, vena cava), (2) blank heart outline with word bank and arrow stickers — student colors/cuts pieces and assembles them into the correct positions on the outline.
designPatterns: Hands-on assembly: color → cut → arrange → glue = kinesthetic learning
Spatial reasoning: which piece goes where?
Word bank + arrows for labeling after assembly
Same anatomy, completely different modality from the posters and diagrams

components.name: Word Search (p22-23)
components.description: Two word search puzzles (different difficulty levels) with heart vocabulary: aorta, artery, atrium, blood, heart, valve, veins.

notes: This is the richest reference yet — a complete mini-curriculum in 24 pages. Carolyng explicitly called out the 'art styles' (plural — the watercolor realistic AND the simplified cross-section) and the 'array of activities' as what she loves. The multi-age design is key: same topic, 12+ activity types, each targeting a different age band and learning modality. The watercolor art is genuinely museum-quality — this isn't clipart, it's hand-painted illustration. Two distinct art styles serve different purposes: watercolor for beauty/reference, simplified for understanding/labeling. The cut-and-assemble craft is the most tactile activity we've seen — it requires the student to physically reconstruct the heart from parts, which is a different kind of understanding than labeling a diagram. This is Carolyng's first drop and it's a unit study, not a single worksheet — she's thinking in curricula, not pages.
